This paper presents AutoEnergyDesign, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) agent reasons over past simulation results, proposes configuration changes and learns in context from each outcome, while a git-based mechanism reverts changes that do not improve the design. The agent couples a reasoning model with explicit memories, a constrained action interface, and an environment-grounded keep/revert feedback signal. The simulator covers eight technologies and computes the 25-year Net Present Cost (NPC). On a case study with measured building loads, the agent, instantiated with three Claude models (Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5; ten runs of 50 simulations each), is compared with random search, Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Bayesian optimization and a (1+1) evolution strategy that shares the agent's acceptance rule (ten seeds of 300 evaluations). With all three models the agent reaches an NPC of 3.53MEUR, 1.20% and 0.23% below the best results of TPE and of the evolution strategy, and comes within 1% of it after a median of 18 to 27.5 simulations; among the baselines, only the evolution strategy does so, after a median of 192 evaluations. In this work, we propose Mixture of Activations (MoA), a token-adaptive FFN design that mixes a dictionary of activation functions using lightweight input-dependent gates while sharing the same linear projections. Theoretically, we establish strict finite-width expressive separations among fixed-activation FFNs, LA, and MoA: LA strictly contains fixed-activation FFNs, while MoA strictly contains LA, with the additional expressivity arising from input-dependent nonlinear hybridization. Empirically, we evaluate MoA through extensive pre-training experiments on dense and MoE language models ranging from 0.12B to 2B parameters under different token budgets, optimizers, and learning rate schedules. MoA consistently achieves lower terminal loss and exhibits more favorable scaling behavior than well-tuned baselines, with minimal parameter and computational overhead. These results suggest that token-adaptive activation mixing is a simple and effective mechanism for improving FFN expressivity in LLMs.

In this paper, we present a mathematically rigorous yet easy-to-compute measure of model complexity that is based on the similarities between feature vectors for different inputs. It is thus well-defined for any parametric model (via NTK feature generalization) and for kernel-based non-parametric models (via the induced kernel). We prove that our measure of complexity generalizes model-specific complexity measures, including polynomial degree (for polynomial regression), kernel length scale (for Matérn kernels), number of neighbors (for k-nearest neighbors), number of splits (for decision trees), and number of trees (for random forests). We also use our measure to obtain new insights into the double descent phenomenon for random Fourier features, random forests, neural networks, and gradient boosting.
♻ ☆ Quantifying Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models ICML 2026
Nail B. Khelifa, Richard E. Turner, Ramji Venkataramanan
Machine learning models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on synthetic data. Recursively training on such data has been observed to significantly degrade performance in a wide range of tasks, often characterized by a progressive drift away from the target distribution. In this work, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon in the setting of score-based diffusion models. For a realistic pipeline where each training round uses a combination of synthetic data and fresh samples from the target distribution, we obtain upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence between the generated and target distributions. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first lower bound on the divergence between the learned and target distributions, even for standard diffusion models. Our results allow us to characterize different regimes of drift, depending on the score estimation error and the proportion of fresh data used in each generation. In a certain regime, the accumulated divergence after several retraining rounds can be expressed as a discounted sum of score estimation errors made at each generation. We also provide empirical results on synthetic data and images to illustrate the theory.

♻ ☆ Prediction-Intervention Games and Invariant Sets

We consider the following two-player game: using observational data, the leader chooses a prediction function for a response variable $Y$ from given covariates. The follower then reacts with an intervention on some covariates in the underlying structural causal model to maximize their own objective. The leader knows the intervention targets, but may have limited knowledge of the follower's objective. We call this setup a prediction-intervention game, a special case of a Stackelberg game. Finding an optimal strategy for the leader is generally difficult. To avoid severe performance loss, the leader may base their prediction on the causal parents of $Y$, or more generally on an invariant subset of covariates. We prove, for two common classes of follower objectives, that predictors based on the stable blanket, an invariant subset, are at least as good as those based on the causal parents. We further upper bound the leader's post-intervention risk by a worst-case risk over allowed interventions and strengthen existing distribution generalization results to analyze this bound: we give sufficient conditions under which stable-blanket predictors are worst-case optimal, and show by examples that these conditions cannot in general be dropped. Finally, we discuss practical strategies for settings with known and unknown graph, and test them on simulated and real-world data.

We apply this decomposition to the score error of trained models and study its quantitative consequences. Since only the gradient component of the error enters the marginal Fokker-Planck dynamics, a model can incur arbitrarily large $L^2$ score error while perfectly matching the target. Starting from this observation, we present three results. First, we derive an upper bound on the Kullback-Leibler divergence that depends only on the observable gradient component of the error. It tightens the standard Girsanov bound for generic score networks and identifies that bound's looseness as the cost of working with path-space rather than marginal-space dynamics. Second, we prove that no non-trivial function of the $L^2$ score error can uniformly lower bound any divergence between the learned and target distributions. Third, we give an estimator of the gradient component, computable from denoising score matching residuals via a dual Sobolev identity, which empirically correlates substantially better with sample quality than the full $L^2$ error.

♻ ☆ A Computable Measure of Suboptimality for Entropy-Regularised Variational Objectives

This increased flexibility introduces a computational challenge, as one loses access to an explicit unnormalised density for the target. To mitigate this difficulty, we introduce a novel measure of suboptimality called 'gradient discrepancy', and in particular a kernel gradient discrepancy (KGD) that can be explicitly computed. In the Bayesian statistics context, KGD coincides with the kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD), and we obtain a novel characterisation of KSD as measuring the size of a variational gradient. Outside this familiar setting, KGD enables novel sampling algorithms to be developed and compared, even when unnormalised densities cannot be obtained. To illustrate this point several novel algorithms are proposed and studied, including a natural generalisation of Stein variational gradient descent, with applications to mean-field neural networks and predictively oriented posteriors presented. On the theoretical side, our principal contribution is to establish sufficient conditions for desirable properties of KGD, such as continuity and convergence control.

♻ ☆ Probabilistic Meshless Methods on Manifolds
Federico Pavesi, Noémie Jaquier, Antonio Candelieri
Probabilistic meshless methods solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by placing a Gaussian process prior on the solution and conditioning it on the PDE at a finite set of collocation nodes. The posterior provides both an approximation of the solution and a Bayesian quantification of its error. While these methods are well established on Euclidean domains, their extension to manifolds lacks, to our knowledge, any convergence analysis. We extend them to compact manifolds and study their convergence in two settings. First, for known manifolds whose Laplace-Beltrami eigenpairs are available, the prior can be evaluated exactly, but the PDE operator generally cannot be applied to it in closed form. We replace this operator by a standard generalized finite difference discretization on a point cloud sampled from the manifold, and show that the resulting method is consistent at the points of the cloud, at a rate governed by their fill distance. Second, for implicit manifolds, known only through a point cloud, both the prior and the operator must be approximated. We propose a new generalized finite difference scheme with a free stencil radius, and show that it retains the consistency of the standard construction while controlling the growth of its coefficients, and that an appropriate radius yields uniform convergence of the discrete Gram matrix. In both settings, we derive error bounds for the posterior mean which separate the collocation error intrinsic to the method from the error due to approximating the operator and, for implicit manifolds, the prior. Experiments on the circle, the sphere and the flat torus confirm our theoretical claims. On real-world cortical thickness data, our approach attains the accuracy of established discretizations, while conditioning on fewer than a tenth of the observations and providing a credible interval at every vertex.

Benedikt Seiter, Anya Fries, Julius von Kügelgen, Jonas Peters
Principal component analysis (PCA) is one of the most widely used unsupervised dimension reduction techniques. We study PCA for data from multiple related domains. Since principal components generally differ across domains, one way to obtain a shared low-rank embedding is to perform PCA on the pooled data. However, this approach can focus on spurious directions that exhibit high variation in only a few domains. To find a robust embedding that still explains most variance in unseen but similar domains, we propose instead to focus on shared directions of variation. To this end, we introduce Anchor PCA which trades off overall explained variance with agreement between the shared and domain-specific low-rank embeddings. Anchor PCA amounts to PCA on a modified target matrix and thus can be solved efficiently. Moreover, we show that Anchor PCA recovers a maximal invariant subspace and admits a minimax reconstruction interpretation under bounded domain-specific covariance inflations. On simulated and real-world data with temporal distribution shift, we demonstrate, respectively, that Anchor PCA recovers the maximal invariant subspace and yields embeddings that explain more variance on unseen domains than the pooling baseline and a worst-case alternative. Taken together, these findings establish Anchor PCA as a promising approach to robust unsupervised dimension reduction from multi-domain data.

♻ ☆ When the Agent Learns Too: Learning to Incentivize with Unobserved Rewards
Ilgin Dogan, Zuo-Jun Max Shen, Anil Aswani
In practice, incentive providers (i.e., principals) often cannot observe the reward realizations of incentivized agents, which is in contrast to many principal-agent models that have been previously studied. This information asymmetry challenges the principal to consistently estimate the agent's unknown rewards by solely watching the agent's decisions, which becomes even more challenging when the agent has to learn its own rewards. This complex setting is observed in various real-life scenarios ranging from renewable energy storage contracts to personalized healthcare incentives. Hence, it offers not only interesting theoretical questions but also wide practical relevance. This paper explores a repeated adverse selection game between a self-interested learning agent and a learning principal. The agent tackles a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to maximize their expected reward plus incentive. On top of the agent's learning, the principal trains a parallel algorithm and faces a trade-off between consistently estimating the agent's unknown rewards and maximizing their own utility by offering adaptive incentives to lead the agent. For a non-parametric model, we introduce an estimator whose only input is the history of principal's incentives and agent's choices. We unite this estimator with a proposed data-driven incentive policy within a MAB framework. Without restricting the type of the agent's algorithm, we prove finite-sample consistency of the estimator and a rigorous regret bound for the principal by considering the sequential externality imposed by the agent. Lastly, our theoretical results are reinforced by simulations justifying applicability of our framework to green energy aggregator contracts.

♻ ☆ Learning to Incentivize Perfect-Knowledge Agents with Unobserved Rewards
Ilgin Dogan, Zuo-Jun Max Shen, Anil Aswani
Motivated by a number of real-world applications from domains like healthcare and sustainable transportation, in this paper we study a scenario of repeated principal-agent games within a multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework, where: the principal gives a different incentive for each bandit arm, the agent picks a bandit arm to maximize its own expected reward plus incentive, and the principal observes which arm is chosen and receives a reward (different than that of the agent) for the chosen arm. Designing policies for the principal is challenging because the principal cannot directly observe the reward that the agent receives for their chosen actions, and so the principal cannot directly learn the expected reward using existing estimation techniques. As a result, the problem of designing policies for this scenario, as well as similar ones, remains mostly unexplored. In this paper, we construct a policy that achieves a low regret (i.e., square-root regret up to a log factor) in this scenario for the case where the agent has perfect-knowledge about its own expected rewards for each bandit arm. We design our policy by first constructing an estimator for the agent's expected reward for each bandit arm. Since our estimator uses as data the sequence of incentives offered and subsequently chosen arms, the principal's estimation can be regarded as an analogy of online inverse optimization in MAB's. Next, we construct a policy that we prove achieves a low regret by deriving finite-sample concentration bounds for our estimator. We conclude with numerical simulations demonstrating the applicability of our framework to personalized adherence-improving incentive design for long-term statin treatments.

♻ ☆ Optimal distribution-free sequential change detection with conformal martingales

For over two decades, the primary existing solution for this problem has employed Vovk's conformal test martingales and associated e-detectors, which control the probability of false alarm (PFA) and the average run length (ARL) respectively. The majority of these works focus on validity, with statistical efficiency usually left for simulations. We develop a comprehensive theory of how conformal p-values behave under non-exchangeable data with a changepoint at an unknown time $T$. We use this to analyze the post-change growth and resulting detection delays and find that the standard existing methods are provably suboptimal for PFA and ARL control, and can lead to delays that are $Ω(T)$ and $Ω(\sqrt{\text{ARL}})$ respectively. We construct new conformal e-processes and e-detectors with learned scores and a fixed, distribution-independent betting dictionary. For any distribution pair with positive finite KL divergence, our methods asymptotically achieve $\log T/\mathrm{KL}$ delay for PFA control and $\log\mathrm{ARL}/\mathrm{KL}$ delay (with a sharp leading constant of 1), which are both proven to be minimax optimal in a suitable double-array framework. Simulations illustrate the large empirical benefits of our new approach.

♻ ☆ Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis
Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Jincheng Ying
Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback--Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Synthetic experiments assess approximation to prescribed tilted targets and sensitivity to the diffusion-step count. Across six offline-to-online continuous-control tasks, the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation achieves higher performance than its offline initialization after online policy improvement.
♻ ☆ Neural Actor--Critic Learning with Minimax Critics and Reflected Langevin Sampling
Kunqi Huang, Lican Kang, Hongrui Shu, Jincheng Ying
Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.

Rather than employing a non-symmetric and high-dimensional non-backtracking operator, a spectral method based on the Bethe-Hessian matrix is conjectured to also reach the Kesten-Stigum detection threshold in the sparse stochastic block model (SBM). Specifically, we demonstrate that: (i) When the expected degree $d\geq 2$, the number of negative outliers of the Bethe-Hessian matrix can consistently estimate the number of blocks above the Kesten-Stigum threshold, thus confirming a conjecture from Saade, Krzakala, and Zdeborová (2014) for $d\geq 2$. (ii) For sufficiently large $d$, its eigenvectors can be used to achieve weak recovery. (iii) As $d\to\infty$, we establish the concentration of the locations of its negative outlier eigenvalues, and weak consistency can be achieved via a spectral method based on the Bethe-Hessian matrix.

♻ ☆ Uniform Race: Parameter-Free Approximate Rejection Sampling
Seiyun Shin, Juhyeong Pang, Kwang-Sung Jun
Consider the approximate sampling problem: given $N$ independent samples from a proposal distribution $μ$, the goal is to select one whose distribution is close to a target $π$ specified only up to a normalizing constant. The seminal work of Block & Polyanskiy (2023) provides a total variation (TV) error bound for approximate rejection sampling (RS) as a function of the algorithm's acceptance threshold $M$. The ideal threshold $M$ that minimizes the bound, however, depends on properties of $(π, μ)$ that are typically unavailable from the observed sample. This raises a natural question: Can one attain the best RS guarantee without taking the best $M$ as input? We answer this question affirmatively by proposing a parameter-free sampling algorithm called uniform race (UR). UR computes a score for each sample $y$ that is the importance weight $π(y)/μ(y)$ divided by an independent uniform random variable and then returns the one with the highest score. We prove that UR attains the best $M$-tuned TV error bound for RS. That is, UR, without knowing the best $M$, achieves the same performance guarantee as RS that takes the best $M$ as input. We also prove that UR has no larger TV error than the budget-calibrated version of the rejection sampler of Rohatgi et al. (2025) and sampling importance resampling (SIR). In particular, we identify instances where UR's error is exponentially smaller in $N$ than that of these two baselines. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which attaining this RS guarantee for every $(π, μ)$ uniquely determines the selection probabilities as those of UR. Finally, test-time scaling experiments on LLM reasoning tasks corroborate the theoretical comparisons and demonstrate that UR remains competitive without requiring threshold selection.

♻ ☆ Understanding Generalization Requires Universal Induction NeurIPS 2026
Aram Ebtekar, Marcus Hutter, Danica J. Sutherland
Classical statistical theory is insufficient to explain the successes of general-purpose AI models, because it depends on handcrafted inductive biases that it cannot justify. No Free Lunch (NFL) theorems force any learner that beats chance on some environments to underperform on others. We might hope that past experience informs which environments to expect, but NFL applies equally to meta-learning. Thus, any method that makes meaningful predictions necessarily begins with an inductive bias external to the data. Choosing to bias toward short programs yields Solomonoff induction (SI), whose performance is competitive against all computable learners - albeit up to "constants" that become large when comparing against specialized methods that exploit background information. We therefore relativize SI to an information vantage point, biasing toward short programs with access to all preexisting information. This reframes the inductive bias: instead of seeking some absolute notion of simplicity, we favour accessibility with respect to our vantage point. An algorithm can only outpredict the relativized SI to the extent that its code contains additional information about the data, and no algorithm can generate such information. While SI is incomputable and hence not a practical algorithm, it provides a formal optimum for inference in the limit of infinite compute, and there is evidence to suggest that frontier AI systems roughly approximate it. Thus, the only known answer to meta-NFL is rooted in algorithmic information theory, which we should expect to play a fundamental role in explaining the generalization behaviour of modern (and future) AI systems.

♻ ☆ Estimating Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning
Joseph H. Rudoler, Kevin Tan, Giles Hooker, Konrad P. Kording
Deep learning systems are known to exhibit implicit regularization (alt. implicit bias), favoring simple solutions instead of merely minimizing the loss function. In some cases, we can analytically derive the implicit regularization -- connecting it to an equivalent penalty that augments the learning objective. However, modern deep learning systems are complex, carrying modifications to the training procedure and architecture (e.g. early stopping, minibatching, dropout) whose effects are not always directly interpretable. Although estimating the resulting implicit regularization could aid theorists in algorithm design and practitioners in interpreting their hyperparameter choices, this problem has received little direct attention. It is also tractable: regularization makes weight updates deviate from loss gradients, promising a signal for identifying implicit bias. Here we provide gradient matching methods that can be used to empirically estimate the implicit regularization. Our method works on networks with known regularization, recovering popular explicit penalties like $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$. It also replicates known implicit effects, like the quadratic weight penalty induced by early stopping in gradient descent, demonstrating that it can be used to test theories of implicit regularization. Crucially, because our method is empirical, it can handle implicit regularization in arbitrary networks. We demonstrate this use by characterizing implicit $\ell_2$ effects of dropout in deep networks. Our work shows that practitioners can use gradient matching to understand regularization in networks with implicit biases that are too complicated to derive analytically.

Fréchet regression, or conditional Barycenters, is a flexible framework for modeling relationships between covariates (usually Euclidean) and response variables on general metric spaces, e.g., probability distributions or positive definite matrices. In this work, we study the existence and computation of conditional barycenters, specifically in the space of positive-definite matrices with the Bures-Wasserstein metric. Moreover, we further characterize the optimization landscape, proving that under this condition, the objective is free of local maxima. Additionally, we develop a projection-free and provably correct algorithm for the approximate computation of first-order stationary points. Finally, we provide a stochastic reformulation that enables the use of off-the-shelf stochastic Riemannian optimization methods for large-scale setups. Numerical experiments validate the performance of the proposed methods on regression problems of real-world biological networks and on large-scale synthetic Diffusion Tensor Imaging problems.

We demonstrate that GO-CBED consistently outperforms existing baselines across various causal reasoning and discovery tasks-including synthetic structural causal models and semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks-particularly in settings with limited experimental budgets and complex causal mechanisms. 2026-11-03
Computer Science and Game Theory
☆ Neural networks and games
Philip R. Neary
Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.
☆ Iterated Elimination of Dominated Mixed Strategies
Federico Echenique, Amanda Friedenberg
This note compares two iterated dominance procedures, one based on eliminating mixed strategies and one based on eliminating pure strategies. It shows that, in compact and continuous games, the mixed-strategy procedure can trail the pure-strategy procedure by at most one round: If the pure-strategy procedure terminates at round $M$, the mixed-strategy procedure terminates at either $M$ or $M+1$, and this bound is tight. It also provides two characterizations of the mixed-strategy procedure that are round-for-round equivalent to it and that require checking for improvements only against opponents' pure strategies.
☆ Learning vs. Optimizing Players in Budgeted Games
Giannis Fikioris, Balasubramanian Sivan, Éva Tardos
We study repeated general games over $T$ rounds between a utility-maximizing optimizer and a learning agent, where budget constraints couple the players' decisions across rounds. Without budgets, low swap regret simultaneously guarantees the learner sublinear regret and caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value. Budgets break this picture: adversarial no-regret becomes impossible, so the natural goals are non-manipulability---no adaptive optimizer earns more than $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + o(T)$, where $\mathtt{BSE}$ is its Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium value---and low stochastic regret when the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy. We give an efficient, budget-feasible learning algorithm that achieves both goals in every budgeted game: any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + O(\sqrt{T})$ in expectation, and if the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret on each such interval. Our learner best responds to forecasts of the optimizer's play that are calibrated in two novel senses, since under budgets the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret. Response calibration, which conditions on the learner's own mixed response by embedding its continuous mixing weight as a step function in $L^2([-1,1])$, prevents manipulation without discretizing responses; dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration ensures low regret. Although low calibration error requires randomized forecasts---distributions over a continuous space that need not have a succinct representation or be directly computable---we construct such forecasts in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.

In this problem, a seller owns an indivisible item, a buyer would like to acquire it, and each of these two traders has a private value for the item and the values are sampled from independent distributions. We ask whether the traders can benefit from a mechanism that burns money, that is, one that charges the buyer more than it pays the seller, so that neither trader enjoys the difference (money burnt is a loss for the traders). Is it possible that the traders will ever be better off if the trade mechanism can burn money? Maybe surprisingly, we show that once a DSIC mechanism can use randomization, money burning can significantly benefit the traders, and the gain of each of them can be arbitrarily large. In contrast, we show that the power of DSIC randomized mechanisms that burn money is still very limited in the sense that they cannot guarantee any constant fraction of the first-best gains-from-trade.

☆ Tight Analysis of Randomized Truthful Scheduling: An $(m+1)/2$ Lower Bound
Wenqian Wang, Chenyang Xu, Yuhao Zhang
The Nisan-Ronen conjecture, a central problem in algorithmic game theory, asserts that no deterministic truthful mechanism for makespan minimization on $m$ unrelated machines can achieve an approximation ratio better than $m$. Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, and Kovács resolved it in 2023, but the optimal approximation ratio achievable by randomized truthful mechanisms remained open. Recently, Anastasiadis, Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, Kovács, and Schecker extended techniques from the deterministic proof to establish a $(3/2-\sqrt{2})(m-1)$ lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms with discrete support and gave a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $m/2+o(m)$. For the broader class of truthful-in-expectation (TIE) mechanisms, however, the gap remained large: the best known upper bound was $(m+5)/2$, while the lower bound was only $2-1/m$. We prove a lower bound of $(m+1)/2$, determining the optimal TIE approximation ratio up to an additive constant as $m/2+Θ(1)$. Our result also improves the leading constant in the lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms from $3/2-\sqrt{2} \approx 0.0858$ to $1/2$. Together with their $m/2+o(m)$ upper bound, our result determines the optimal approximation ratio for universally truthful mechanisms up to lower-order terms.

☆ Sharp Bounds for Truthful-in-Expectation Scheduling
Yunpeng Li
We study randomized mechanisms for scheduling indivisible jobs on $n$ unrelated machines. Each machine is controlled by a selfish agent who privately knows its processing time for each job. A mechanism assigns every job to a machine and makes payments. We require truthfulness in expectation: no agent can increase its expected payment minus its expected processing cost by misreporting, regardless of the other agents' reports. The makespan is the maximum total processing time assigned to a machine; the objective is to minimize its expectation. We prove that the optimal approximation ratio is $(n+1)/2$ for every $n\ge7$, relative to the minimum makespan of an integral assignment. The lower bound holds for every $n$ and allows unrestricted computation and arbitrary correlations among assignments, assuming finite expected payments and a guarantee uniform over all finite job counts. The matching mechanism uses correlated rounding and runs in expected polynomial bit time on rational inputs. These guarantees hold for all finite nonnegative processing times. For two machines, we characterize the optimal approximation ratio exactly as an analytic constant, approximately $1.505995705434$, and give a mechanism attaining it. For three machines the optimal ratio is $2$. For four, five, and six machines we obtain upper bounds of $3$, $105/32$, and $29/8$, respectively, compared with the general lower bound $(n+1)/2$. The proofs for $n\ge7$ do not rely on computer-assisted certificates; the two- and three-machine results use exact rational computer-assisted certificates.
☆ Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs STOC 2027
Krzysztof Rogowski, Marcin Dziubiński
We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents. For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates. For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio. We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure. Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

☆ Toward Constant-Factor Maximin Share Guarantees for Subadditive Valuations
Bo Li, Ankang Sun
For $n$ agents and $m$ indivisible goods, an agent's maximin share (MMS) is the largest minimum bundle value she can obtain by partitioning the goods into $n$ bundles. Constant MMS approximations are known for additive, submodular, or XOS valuations, but whether such a guarantee exists for general subadditive valuations remains open. We advance this question in two directions. For general subadditive valuations, we exponentially improve the guarantee from $Ω(1/\log\log n)$ to $Ω(1/\log^* n)$, where $\log^* n$ is the iterated logarithm. We then seek constant MMS guarantees under additional structure on subadditive valuations by studying $q$-partitioning valuations: every partition of a bundle into at most $q$ groups admits nonnegative group prices that sum to the bundle's value and whose sum on any collection of groups is at most the value of their union. This hierarchy ranges from subadditivity at $q=2$ to XOS for $q\ge m$. We give the first study of MMS in the intermediate classes and prove constant guarantees whenever $q/n$ has a fixed positive lower bound, including $1/6$ for $q\ge n$ and $1/4$ for $q\ge2n$. For XOS valuations, we further improve the universal guarantee from $4/17\approx 0.2353$ to $5/16=0.3125$. For subadditive valuations, we prove a bidding amplification theorem that gives an exponential bound on each agent's probability of receiving less than half her MMS, while satisfying her budget in every outcome. For $q$-partitioning valuations, we give a scalar criterion that converts bounds on the value lost from disjoint deletions within a bundle into bounds on potential losses, even when an agent contributes zero below the target bundle value. For XOS valuations, we prove a reservation theorem that selects goods for integral assignment together with auxiliary additive valuations and accounts for the loss in rounding.
☆ Linear Equivalence of Full Weight Spectrum Cyclic Orbit Codes
Minjia Shi, Ferruh Ozbudak
We determine the linear-equivalence classes within the two families of full weight spectrum one-orbit cyclic subspace codes. This solves the second open problem posed by Castello, Polverino and Zullo [J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 212 (2025) 106005]. For the first family, the criterion is a fractional linear transformation over $\F_q$ followed by a power of $q$-Frobenius. For the second family, it is an affine transformation over $\F_{q^2}$ together with a power of $q$-Frobenius. We use polynomial spaces over finite fields, the linear-isometry theorem for cyclic orbit codes, and trace duality. The arguments include parameters belonging to proper subfields of the ambient field.

☆ The Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids
Max Klimm, Paul Lippke, Philipp Warode
We study optimal contracts when an agent allocates continuous effort subject to polymatroid capacity constraints. Effort produces a linear expected reward and incurs a cost. With binary outcomes and limited liability, the principal chooses a single reward share. For linear costs, an optimal contract can be computed in polynomial time. For quadratic costs, the agent has a unique best response computable by polynomially many submodular minimizations, yet optimizing the principal's share is NP-hard even for explicitly represented cut-based rank functions. With $n$ activities, the best-response path can have $2^{n-O(\log n)}$ breakpoints even when each reward coefficient and each rank value is an integer representable in $O(n\log n)$ bits. The construction also answers a question of Allman, Lo, and McCormick on polynomial bit length for source-sink monotone two-parameter minimum cuts. Despite this complexity, an optimal contract for quadratic costs always exists with a share of at most $1/2$. Consequently, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ best-response computations suffice for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation. For rational quadratic costs on explicitly described rational polytopes containing zero, this gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. More generally, a share of at most $1/p$ suffices for continuous convex costs homogeneous of degree $p>1$, on any compact convex action set containing zero. For general convex costs with an exact value and bounded-subgradient oracle, we obtain an oracle approximation scheme using approximate best responses and a supplied lower bound on positive welfare.

☆ Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
Zehan Lin, Xiaowei Wu, Shengwei Zhou
We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

☆ Robust Aggregation of Quantile Statistics: from Median to Interval
Mingyu Song, Yizhou Wang, Yuqing Kong
Quantile-based summaries, such as prediction intervals and medians, are commonly used in economic forecasting, climate science, and public health. For highly skewed samples, experimental evidence suggests that estimates of the mean can be biased toward the median, whereas estimates of the median are relatively accurate. This motivates aggregating explicitly elicited quantiles rather than reported means. We study robust aggregation of quantile reports for bounded outcomes under squared loss, minimizing worst-case regret relative to an omniscient Bayesian aggregator who knows the information structure and observes all private signals. Without restrictions on the information structure, no rule improves on the constant forecast at the range midpoint in worst-case regret. We therefore consider weak substitutes, a diminishing-returns condition on the value of information, and characterize optimal aggregation rules under this condition. For central prediction intervals with common nominal coverage $α$, the optimal rule, which we call regularized simple average for prediction intervals, shrinks the average reported interval midpoint toward the range midpoint, with a weight determined by $α$ and the number $n$ of experts. This optimal rule strictly improves on the constant baseline in worst-case regret when $α<1/\sqrt{n}$; at or above this threshold, the constant rule is optimal. The optimal worst-case regret is minimized at a unique interior coverage level, revealing a nonmonotonic relationship between coverage and aggregation performance. For median reports, regularized simple average for medians similarly shrinks the average reported median toward the range midpoint, assigning weight $1/n$ to the reported average and strictly improving on the constant baseline in worst-case regret for every finite $n\ge2$.

☆ Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents
Yosef Zumer, Erel Segal-Halevi, David Sarne
Bankruptcy rules are rules for dividing an insufficient estate among people with different claims. Existing rules assume that the claims are publicly known. When this is not the case, claimants have a strong incentive to claim more than they are due, as bankruptcy rules give larger allocations to claimants with larger claims. A remedy often used by legal systems is to make over-reporting costly by requiring evidence and imposing penalties. But this remedy also increases the legal expenses of proving true claims, which might result in under-reporting. Encouraging true reporting requires fine-tuning of the legal costs. This paper incorporates the costs of supporting both true and false claims into the bankruptcy model. Claimants incur costs for the true and false parts of their claims, with false claims costing at least as much per unit as true claims. The goal is to set cost rates that induce claimants to report their true entitlements, neither more nor less. Whether this is possible depends on the allocation rule. The proportional and constrained equal awards rules cannot guarantee truthfulness at any positive true-claim cost rate; the same holds for constrained equal losses with at least three claimants. For $N\ge2$ claimants, the rule TAL-1/N from the parameterized Talmud family induces truthfulness exactly when the true-claim cost rate is at most 1/N and the false-claim cost rate is at least 1-1/N. This rule is optimal in the sense that its truthful cost region contains that of every piecewise smooth allocation rule: it gives the legal system the maximum possible flexibility in setting the legal costs. For two claimants, TAL-1/2 (aka Contested Garment rule) uniquely attains this optimal region.
☆ Logarithmic Comparison-Query Complexity for EF1 Allocations
Zehan Lin, Shengxin Liu, Biaoshuai Tao, Shengwei Zhou
We study the comparison-query complexity of computing allocations that are envy-free up to one item (EF1) for $n$ agents with heterogeneous additive preferences over $m$ indivisible items. In this model, the algorithm may only query which of two bundles an agent prefers, without ever observing numerical valuations or costs. Prior work established $O(\log m)$ query bounds for at most three agents, leaving open whether query complexity logarithmic in $m$ is achievable for every fixed $n \ge 4$. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for every fixed $n\ge2$, we design algorithms that compute EF1 allocations using $O(\log m)$ comparison queries, matching the known $Ω(\log m)$ lower bound. Our results hold for both chores with nonnegative costs and goods with nonnegative valuations.
☆ Designing AI-Mediated Communication in Teams
Wichinpong Park Sinchaisri, Zhiwei Wang
AI assistants increasingly participate in work that requires employees to exchange information and coordinate decisions. We study how a firm should design this communication when workers' interests conflict with each other's and the firm's. Two workers privately know local conditions and their preferred responses, while the assistant knows aggregate project conditions. The firm discloses project information before workers report and choose their own actions. Transparency improves adaptation but can undermine truthful preference reporting. When workers agree with the firm on the productive direction, coarsening project information under weak coordination can preserve useful preference reporting at a cost in forecast precision. Under strong coordination, the firm instead prefers full project disclosure and factual reports, because preference information induces costly accommodation of private objectives. Under weak coordination, a firm-optimal policy can leave workers worse off than direct exchange; requiring their acceptance can call for further coarsening. Releasing project context after reports can sustain factual communication that early release would prevent. With separate delivery decisions that cannot be revised jointly, endogenous forwarding weakly improves firm-preferred performance over unchanged forwarding and strictly improves it in some environments. Numerical comparisons show that full initial disclosure captures most gains in the aligned environments considered, while further design has greater value when workers can favor opposing directions. The results distinguish the credibility of employees' reports from their organizational value and show how disclosure timing affects both.
☆ Coercive at the equilibrium, monotone nowhere: exact convergence certificates for learning in first-price auctions
Benjamin Lubin
The Bayes-Nash equilibria of an auction are the solutions of a variational inequality, and for standard auctions its operator fails every monotonicity notion, so the theory of monotone operators is unavailable to learning in auctions. We show what replaces monotonicity for the first-price auction: a certificate that is strong but local. For uniform values the single-population operator has an exact closed form and an exact Minty identity at the equilibrium; for two bidders its Gateaux derivative there is $L^2$-coercive with best constant exactly one in every piecewise-linear bid space with $m$ pieces, while the Minty inequality holds only on a ball whose radius decays like $m^{-5/2}$. The decay is exact: $m^{5/2}$ times the radius converges to $1/(8 \cdot 3^{1/4})$, and the worst perturbations converge to an alternating geometric profile with ratio $-(2-\sqrt{3})$. Refinement shrinks the ball, not the constant; independent learners see the same constant. For a general prior and bidder count there are two certificates, at the true equilibrium and at the equilibrium of the finite-dimensional bid space a learning algorithm runs in. The first is an explicit weight $w_F$, positive for every log-concave prior, equal to the second exactly for the value distributions $F(v)=v^a$. Otherwise the learners' certificate differs by knot masses, because the discretized equilibrium's slopes oscillate with a law proved for two and three bidders, and for four under a computer-verified bottom layer. The limit of the learners' certificate is proved in closed form, a function of the prior alone, and characterizes positivity: positive uniformly in $m$ in the limit exactly when that minimum is positive, with a known rate; for one prior at every $m$ by interval arithmetic. For more bidders the limit is conjectured. The exact identities and leading-order inequalities are machine-checked in Lean.
☆ Balanced Fair Division and Generalized Kneser Graphs
Sharareh Alipour, Amir Jafari
We study indivisible goods allocated to two prescribed nonempty groups whose members have arbitrary monotone valuations. Via the connection of Kyropoulou, Suksompong, and Voudouris, these guarantees follow from chromatic bounds for $\mathrm{KG}(2n,n,r)$, whose vertices are $n$-subsets of a $2n$-set, adjacent when their intersection has size less than $r$. We prove its chromatic number is six for $r=2$, $n\ge2$, resolving Jafari and Alipour's conjecture, and at least ten for $r=3$, $n\ge4$, improving the previous lower bound of six; the known upper bound is fourteen. We show that the standard box-complex $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index bound yields exactly five and nine for $n\ge3$ and $n\ge5$, respectively. To exceed these bounds, we exploit restrictions on maps induced by colorings: a proper five- or nine-coloring must induce a nonzero homology map, yet local constraints force all generators, supported on pentagon or rook configurations, to map to zero. The ten-color proof compares integral and fractional common centers using a sharp rounding theorem for five subset constraints. A linear-time retraction from the full allocation graph onto balanced layers adds cardinality balance to known nonlinear discrepancy guarantees. For each fixed removal allowance in the guaranteed-existence range, finding a balanced fair allocation or an explicit monotonicity violation from valuation circuits is polynomial-time equivalent to finding a monochromatic edge in a circuit-specified coloring of the corresponding graph. The reverse reduction produces normalized monotone binary valuations using ordinary circuits.
☆ On the Complexity of Exact Autobidding Equilibria
Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan
Autobidding equilibria link advertisers' value multipliers or participation probabilities through aggregate budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints. We establish the exact computational complexity of finding these equilibria across several canonical settings: exact equilibrium computation is $\mathsf{FIXP}$-complete for second-price ROI pacing, budget- or ROI-constrained generalized second-price (GSP) sponsored shopping, and second-price throttling. Furthermore, approximating the equilibrium control vector in distance to a true equilibrium is $\mathsf{FIXP}_{a}$-complete when the target accuracy is provided as input.

☆ On the Role of Geometry in Solving Variational Inequalities
Ioannis Anagnostides, Ioannis Panageas, Jingming Yan
The geometry of constraints in variational inequalities (VIs) plays a central role in applications ranging from resource allocation and equilibrium computation to constrained optimization. Yet, its effect on computational complexity has received surprisingly little attention beyond special cases. We examine this question when the constraint set is an $\ell_p$ ball. This family of problems encompasses two of the most extensively studied classes of problems in algorithmic game theory: symmetric bimatrix games for $p = 1$ and multi-player polymatrix games for $p = \infty$. Both of these problems are known to be PPAD-complete even for affine operators. We establish a comprehensive complexity landscape for VIs over $\ell_p$ balls across the full range $p\in[1,\infty]$. First, for any $p\neq 2$, we show that finding an inverse-polynomial approximate VI solution is PPAD-complete even for affine operators. In contrast, for $p=2$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for affine VIs, extending a classic result of Ye (1992) beyond symmetric operators. On the other hand, once the operator becomes quadratic, we establish PPAD-completeness even at inverse polynomial precision. From a technical standpoint, we develop a new toolkit for exploiting the geometry of the constraint set and the structure of the operator to characterize the complexity of equilibrium and optimization problems, which is of independent interest.
♻ ☆ A Game-Theoretic Decision Framework for Optimal Selection of Coordination Detection Methods in Multi-UAV Fleet Operations
Christian Manasseh, Savana Ammons
Detecting coordination among unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) fleets operating in shared airspace and identifying the route-lead aircraft whose navigation decisions govern fleet behavior presents a fundamental speed--accuracy trade-off: fast methods enable real-time traffic management but sacrifice detection fidelity, while accurate methods may exceed the time budget for actionable airspace deconfliction. This paper presents a game-theoretic decision framework that resolves this trade-off by formulating method selection as a two-player zero-sum game between a Monitor (selecting computational methods and parameters) and Nature (selecting the unknown traffic scenario). We construct an end-to-end pipeline from trajectory surveillance data through eight candidate detection algorithms, a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis characterizing their stochastic performance, and finally a multi-objective optimization layer that identifies Pareto-optimal method portfolios. The minimax solution provides a robust mixed strategy with a probability distribution over methods that guarantees worst-case performance regardless of scenario uncertainty. Experimental evaluation across 200 randomized configurations spanning 5--50 aircraft demonstrates that the framework recommends distinct method portfolios depending on operational priority: Koopman Phase dominates balanced (70.6%) and speed-priority (79.7%) profiles, while CRQA emerges as primary (47.4%) when route-lead identification is prioritized. The framework achieves a guaranteed game value of 0.29--0.53 (normalized utility) across all tested preference profiles, providing the first principled, scenario-adaptive methodology for computational method selection in UTM fleet monitoring operations.
♻ ☆ Coalitions, Stability, and Majority Jackpots: Frameworks for Unifying Majoritarian and Proportional Allocation in Multiwinner Elections
Kit Scriven, Nitin Kohli
Social choice literature on multiwinner elections tends to focus on characterizing two distinct tasks: majoritarian representation and proportional representation. However, many real world systems can be viewed as operating between these two extremes, such as majority jackpot systems used in several countries throughout history. Towards the goal of better understanding these systems from a social choice perspective, we introduce two frameworks that encompass existing desiderata for majoritarian and proportional settings: coalitions, which encompasses properties such as fixed majority and solid coalitions; and stability, which encompasses various generalizations of Condorcet's criterion for single-winner elections, such as Gehrlein stability and local stability, among others. We develop theory and tools that characterize the mathematical and computational aspects of both frameworks across a wide array of preference structures (such as the unrestricted domain over candidates and the restricted domain of party lists). Building on this foundation, we shed new light on majority jackpot electoral systems, which to date have received limited mathematical analysis in the social choice literature.
♻ ☆ A Bulow-Klemperer Theorem for Bundling and Improved Approximation Bounds for Simple Auctions

We study simple auctions for one additive bidder whose values for $m$ items are independent. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{BSPA}_2 \le 2\,\mathrm{BREV}$. Thus, one additional bidder lets a reserve-free second-price auction for the grand bundle match the optimal revenue from one bidder, regardless of the number of items. This gives a Bulow-Klemperer theorem for bundling and resolves an open question of Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, and Weinberg (EC 2025) on whether constant competition suffices for bundling. The factor-$2$ bundling approximation is also tight. For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{π^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). For the lower bound, we construct an instance in which pricing three disjoint bundles earns more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). Together, these results narrow the tight approximation ratio to the range $[2.11, 2.645]$.

Shadeeb Hossain, Elias Calboreanu, Kristopher Wilson
The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.

♻ ☆ Learning vs. Optimizing Bidders in Budgeted Auctions
Giannis Fikioris, Balasubramanian Sivan, Éva Tardos
The study of repeated interactions between a learner and a utility-maximizing optimizer has yielded deep insights into the manipulability of learning algorithms. However, existing literature primarily focuses on independent, unlinked rounds, largely ignoring the ubiquitous practical reality of budget constraints. In this paper, we study this interaction in repeated second-price auctions in a Bayesian setting between a learning agent and a strategic agent, both subject to strict budget constraints, showing that such cross-round constraints fundamentally alter the strategic landscape. First, we generalize the classic Stackelberg equilibrium to the Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium. We prove that an optimizer's optimal strategy in a budgeted setting requires time-multiplexing; for a $k$-dimensional budget constraint, the optimal strategy strictly decomposes into up to $k+1$ distinct phases, with each phase employing a possibly unique mixed strategy (the case of $k=0$ recovers the classic Stackelberg equilibrium where the optimizer repeatedly uses a single mixed strategy). Second, we address the intriguing question of non-manipulability. We prove that when the learner employs a standard Proportional controller (the "P" of the PID-controller) to pace their bids, the optimizer's utility is upper bounded by their objective value in the Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium baseline. By bounding the dynamics of the PID controller via a novel analysis, our results establish that this widely used control-theoretic heuristic is actually strategically robust.
♻ ☆ Pareto-optimal Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling with Predictions
Ziyad Benomar, Vianney Perchet
We study preemptive single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\varepsilon$ is achievable with robustness $\varepsilon^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions. Furthermore, we give a simple randomized algorithm, using predicted sizes, with consistency $1+\varepsilon$ and robustness $(3\varepsilon)^{-1/2}+O(1)$, strictly below the deterministic frontier. The question of determining the Pareto-optimal frontier among randomized algorithms remains open.

Yiannis Giannakopoulos, Johannes Hahn
We study the classical multi-item monopoly setting with a single additive buyer and $m$ heterogeneous items whose values are independent but not necessarily identically distributed. We compare the revenue (REV) of the optimal truthful auction, which in general may be randomized or complicated, with the revenues of three simple deterministic auctions: selling all items separately (SREV), selling them as a single grand bundle (BREV), and choosing the better of the two. Our technical cornerstone is a general upper bound on the optimal multidimensional revenue, parameterized by freely chosen item-wise caps, and expressed in terms of optimal single-item, Myersonian revenues and basic statistics of the value distributions. We derive this inequality through Lagrangian duality for a nonlinear programming formulation of the worst-case approximation ratio of separate-selling. Combining this inequality with carefully chosen caps and a probabilistic analysis of the resulting terms, we obtain improved approximation guarantees for all three deterministic auctions, both for general independent values and for iid values. Notably, we prove that $REV\le 2.5\max\{SREV,BREV\}$, improving the long-standing $5.2$ factor of Ma and Simchi-Levi and the $6$ factor of Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg. We complement this upper bound with a construction establishing a lower bound of $2.19$, improving the bound of $2$ by Rubinstein. For two iid items, we determine the exact approximation ratio of selling separately. Our proof constructs tight Lagrangian dual certificates for the aforementioned programming formulation, when item values lie in the grid $\{0,1/K,2/K,\dots,1\}$, for any discretization parameter $K$. Taking $K\to\infty$ yields the tight ratio $1+W(1/e)\approx1.2785$ in the continuous-valued setting, where $W$ is the Lambert-W function, closing the $[1.278,1.368]$ gap left by Hart and Nisan.

The improved upper bounds use a new capped revenue inequality obtained via a new Lagrangian dual construction
♻ ☆ Payoff scaling shapes cooperation in LLM agents across languages
Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Thanh-Bang Cao, Phong-Hao Le, Hong-Dan Nguyen, Phu-Quy Nguyen-Lam, Minh-Luan Nguyen-Vo, Hong-Phat Pham, Phu-Hoa Pham, Thien-Kim Than, Chi-Nguyen Tran, Huy Tran, Gia-Thoai Tran-Le, Alessio Buscemi, Le Hong Trang, The Anh Han
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that negotiate, coordinate, and make decisions on behalf of human users. Understanding how they cooperate is therefore important for AI governance and machine behaviour research. We examine two factors: payoff magnitude and interaction language. Classical game theory predicts that multiplying all payoffs by a positive constant should not change behaviour because the underlying strategic incentives remain unchanged. We test this prediction using five widely adopted commercial LLMs playing an iterated prisoner's dilemma across ten payoff scales and five languages (English, French, Vietnamese, Chinese and Arabic). Contrary to theoretical expectations, changing only the numerical scale of payoffs substantially alters cooperation. Models respond differently, often in opposite directions, meaning that averages across models can conceal important behavioural heterogeneity. Sensitivity to payoff scale also depends strongly on prompt language. Moreover, payoff scale modifies the effects of persona instructions: at sub-unit stakes, where no payoff shown exceeds 1, all five models cooperate more under a selfish than a cooperative persona, whereas Claude and Gemini reverse this pattern at larger scales. These findings show that cooperation measures depend critically on payoff scale and language and should not be treated as fixed model traits.

♻ ☆ Project Submission Games in Participatory Budgeting
Piotr Faliszewski, Łukasz Janeczko, Andrzej Kaczmarczyk, Grzegorz Lisowski, Grzegorz Pierczyński
We introduce the framework of project submission games, capturing the behavior of project proposers in participatory budgeting (and multiwinner elections). Here, each proposer submits a subset of project proposals, aiming at maximizing the total cost of those that get funded. We focus on finding conditions under which pure Nash equilibria (NE) exist in our games, and on the complexity of checking whether they exist. We also seek algorithms for computing best responses for the proposers
♻ ☆ Fair Division with Binary Valuations: Characterizations
Florian Brandl, Warut Suksompong, Nicholas Teh
We consider the fair allocation of indivisible goods with binary valuations. In this setting, the maximum Nash welfare rule, the leximin rule, and all additive welfarist rules with a strictly concave function coincide. We show that for any number of agents, this rule is the only rule that satisfies envy-freeness up to one good, strategyproofness, neutrality, minimal completeness, and invariance under disapproving unassigned goods (IDU). Moreover, we present an alternative characterization for two agents, where we replace IDU with non-redundancy and resource-monotonicity. In both characterizations, all axioms are necessary.

♻ ☆ Exploring the Tractability Frontier of Hylland-Zeckhauser Models
Ioannis Panageas, Avi Shein, Shayan Taherijam, Vijay V. Vazirani
The Hylland-Zeckhauser (HZ) mechanism provides a market-based approach to one-sided matching, making efficient equilibrium computation central to its implementation. Under bi-valued utilities, it admits a strongly polynomial-time algorithm [VY], whereas with four values per buyer, the problem is PPAD-hard under inverse polynomial approximation [CCPY]. To understand the tractability boundary, we study two extensions of the bi-valued case: a third linear utility value and separable concave utilities with two common slopes. For every fixed rational $a\in(0,1)$, we prove that computing a normalized additive $\varepsilon_{*}(a)/N$-equilibrium in an $N$-buyer HZ market is PPAD-complete for some constant $\varepsilon_{*}(a)>0$, even when all utilities belong to the same prescribed set $\{0,a,1\}$. This resolves the main question left open by [VY, CCPY]: whether three utility values already suffice for PPAD-hardness. Assuming the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture, we strengthen the above-stated result to constant additive-error hardness. For the concave extension, we compute an exact equilibrium in strongly polynomial time with two marginal utility slopes common across goods for each buyer and arbitrary rational buyer-good breakpoints. With three common marginal slopes, suitable breakpoints encode the three valued linear case, yielding PPAD-hardness. Thus, our paper identifies two thresholds separating tractable and intractable cases of HZ models with utility functions specified by utility values or marginal slopes. In both cases, the tractability threshold lies between two and three.
♻ ☆ Domination-Avoiding Learning Agents Cannot Collude NeurIPS 2026
Noam Nisan, Emmanuel Zerah
An influential paper of Calvano et al. empirically demonstrated that Q-learning agents spontaneously collude when placed as sellers that compete on prices in a natural market model. More recent results of Fish et al. empirically demonstrated that similar collusion happens with commercial LLMs. We formally prove that such collusion can also happen with external-regret-minimizing agents. We identify a very general class of agents, which we term Domination-Avoiding agents, that provably do not collude in such markets. This class contains all Mean-Based agents and all internal-regret-minimizing agents, as well as others such as Multiplicative-Weight agents with variable learning rate and contextual variants thereof. More generally we show that, in any game, this class of agents is guaranteed to jointly learn to almost never play strategies that are eliminated by repeated elimination of purely dominated strategies.

♻ ☆ Existence of the Core in Approval-Based Committee Elections
Patrick Becker, Matthias Greger, Dominik Peters
We resolve the central open question in the theory of approval-based committee elections: we prove that the core is always non-empty. This means that there always exists a committee for which no coalition of voters can deviate to an alternative committee of proportional size that every member strictly prefers. This property was introduced by Aziz et al. (2017) to capture proportional representation and coalitional stability, but no known algorithm achieved it except up to a constant approximation factor or in special cases. Our approach begins by strengthening the core to core+, which requires the committee to be robust even to fractional deviations. Using LP duality, this property can equivalently be defined in terms of a payment-based certificate under which no losing candidate gathers too much support. We then define a voting rule that chooses a committee admitting a certificate that maximizes a novel harmonic entropy objective function, which rewards balanced payment distributions. We show that the payment system associated with an optimal committee certifies that the committee satisfies core+, establishing existence. The same is true for local optima, which allows us to design a polynomial-time algorithm computing a core+ committee.

♻ ☆ Settling the Complexity of Hylland--Zeckhauser Equilibria
Zhengyang Liu, Yixin Tao, Yonglei Yan
The Hylland--Zeckhauser (HZ) mechanism is a foundational framework for allocating indivisible goods in one-sided matching markets via lotteries supported by competitive prices and equal artificial budgets. We resolve the exact computational complexity of the HZ scheme by proving that computing an exact HZ equilibrium is FIXP-complete, thereby settling a conjecture of Vazirani and Yannakakis. Notably, this hardness persists even when computing the equilibrium allocation alone. We establish our hardness result via a reduction that encodes quadratic fixed-point equations into a reciprocal variational inequality. On the algorithmic side, we present a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm that achieves an additive error of $0.0755211 + δ$ for any $δ> 0$, significantly improving upon the previous $1/e$ guarantee.
